newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU caught between trade foes over wheat exports.
newsitem.headline: EU caught between trade foes over wheat exports.

text.p: The European Union, which has fought endless trade battles to sell grain with subsidies, thought its problems were over when it struck a deal with the United States not to undercut American farmers.
Now, in an abrupt shift of trade power, southern hemisphere producers like Australia are starting to flood the world market and pressure is building on Brussels to put its farmers first.

"We have had a consistent policy of selling at high prices when our competitors are undercutting the market to win back their share," a dissatisifed grain official in an EU member country said on Wednesday, asking not to be identified.
At stake is the fate of four million tonnes of wheat worth half a billion dollars still unsold from last year's crop, which the EU needs to sell just as the competition reaches full swing.

Australia is just finishing its largest harvest on record. Weeks ago, Argentina also reaped its biggest crop. Both have been using a hard sales pitch to woo importers, at times encroaching on African markets the EU regards as its own.

Now, according to some traders and officials, the EU faces the dilemma of either reviewing its pledge to the United States through increased export subsidies, or failing to sell wheat and perhaps storing it at even greater cost to taxpayers.
The EU's problem, they argue, is that prices in the U.S. have not kept pace with a fall in world markets because it was one of the few producers not to report a large crop last year.
In contrast, Europe had a near-record harvest last summer and the quality produced was below average -- both factors which would normally force it to drop prices.
"We have a problem this year because we have demand for our wheat but Argentina and Australia have been selling like crazy. That's where the real world market has been," the official said.

The EU made its pledge not to undercut U.S. farmers late last year after U.S. grain exporters reacted furiously when it restored export subsidies to cope with a collapse in world prices from record levels.
In exchange Washington resisted domestic calls to restore its own subsidies, fearing that would inflate local prices, suck in cheap wheat from Canada and create another trade headache.
Both sides are trying to avoid a repeat of past subsidy wars that cost billions of dollars and encouraged unwanted grain.

Yet some European officials pine for an era when the United States was market enemy number one -- not Australia whose sales are often kept secret. "We knew where we stood then. This whole U.S. business has made it harder for us," said one official.
Australia says it competes openly on the international market and has in turn attacked EU subsidies as a distortion.
The EU signalled its intention to tough out the competition on Tuesday when an official in Brussels ruled out using heavy export subsidies to help farmers compete head-on with Australia.
With its August harvest, the EU had a four-month head start over its southern rivals and has sold two thirds of the export wheat available from last year's crop, or six million tonnes.

Traders say the gamble to keep the peace with Washington could still pay off if demand from traditional North African customers holds up, or if Iraq continues to favour France with its United Nations oil-for-food purchases.
Some suspect Brussels of soft-pedalling exports to assist a policy of depressing high internal prices, another key mission.
But traders agree the time for exports may be running out. Competition will be even fiercer in the spring when Canadian rivers thaw and any unsold wheat will likely go into storage.
